items.e: **The place and time of breaking the bread, and who breaks it – containing 20 sections:** One should break the bread at the place where it is well baked. (And with our bread, one should break it on the side of the loaf and cut slightly from the top and bottom—Hagahot Maimoni, chapter 7 of Hilchot Berachot). He should cut the piece to be broken, and he must cut it slightly, so that if he were to hold the slice, the rest of the loaf would be lifted with it. For if not, it is considered as already sliced. He should leave it attached to the loaf and begin the blessing, and after he concludes the blessing, he should separate it—so that the blessing concludes while the bread is still whole. And he should not break off a piece that is too small, because that appears stingy, nor a piece larger than the size of a kebeitza (an egg), because that appears gluttonous. Rema: On Shabbat, one should not cut the loaf before the blessing, so that the loaves remain whole (Tosafot and Mordechai, chapter "Keitzad Mevarchin"). Nevertheless, if he forgot and cut it as on a weekday, it is not harmful (Mordechai). And it seems that the restriction not to break more than a kebeitza applies only on weekdays and when eating alone, but on Shabbat or when eating with many people—and he must give each person a kezayit—it is permitted to break off as much as needed. See also Siman 274.

Bless "Who takes out bread from the ground" (And if many people are eating together, the people dining should direct their heart (intention) to the person saying the beracha, and answer amen, and the person saying the beracha should give intention to the amen)(Or Zarua) . And one pauses slightly between the word "lechem" [bread] and the word "min" [from].
Do not bless "Hamotzi" before grasping the bread.

Put both hands on the bread when you are about to bless "Hamotzi"; for the 10 fingers are reflective of the 10 mitzvot that are dependent on bread. Additionally, there are 10 words in the blessing of "Hamotzi" and 10 words in the following verses: Psalms 104:14, "He causes the grass to grow for the cattle, and grass for the service of man: that he may bring forth bread out of the land." Psalms 145:15, "The eyes of all look to you expectantly, and you give them their food at the proper time." Deuteronomy 8:8, "A land of wheat and barley, of vines, figs, and pomegranates, a land of olive trees and honey." Bresheit 27:28, "May G!d give you from the dew of heaven and fat of the earth, and an abundance of grain and wine."

He should not break (the bread) until they bring before him salt or a condiment (Rashi explains: anything that is eaten with bread) with which to dip the piece of bread. But if the bread is clean (i.e., of fine quality) or seasoned with spices or salt like ours, or if he intends to eat dry bread, he does not need to wait. Rema: Nevertheless, it is a mitzvah to bring salt to every table before breaking the bread, because the table is likened to the altar and the eating to a sacrifice, and it is said, "On all your offerings you shall offer salt" (Beit Yosef in the name of Shibbolei HaLeket). And it protects from calamity (Tosafot and Hagahot Ashri, chapter "Keitzad Mevarchin", and see the end of Siman 170).

He should eat immediately and not speak between the blessing and the eating. If he did speak, he must recite the blessing again—unless the speech was related to matters connected to what he blessed over. For example, if he blessed over the bread and before eating said, "Bring salt" or "Bring a condiment," or "Give so-and-so to eat," or "Give food to the animal," and the like—he does not need to bless again. Rema: Nevertheless, ideally one should not interrupt at all (Kol Bo). And the ruling that if he spoke idle words he must bless again applies only if the one who broke the bread spoke before he ate. But if he spoke afterward, it is not considered an interrupting speech—even if the other participants have not yet eaten—since they already fulfilled their obligation through the eating of the one who broke the bread. For they are not required to eat from his piece; they do so only to enhance the mitzvah (Rokeach and Or Zarua).

If Reuven was washing his hands for eating, and Yaakov was reciting the HaMotzi blessing with the intention to fulfill the obligation on behalf of the listeners, and afterward Reuven dried his hands and recited the blessing over washing hands (Al Netilat Yadayim)—this is not considered an interruption, and he fulfills his obligation with Yaakov’s HaMotzi blessing and does not need to recite the HaMotzi blessing again.

If one forgot and ate without reciting the HaMotzi blessing, then if he remembers during the meal, he should recite the blessing. But if he only remembers after he has finished his meal, he does not recite the blessing.
If one is in doubt whether or not he recited the HaMotzi blessing, he does not go back and recite the blessing.

If, instead of the HaMotzi blessing, he recited Shehakol Nihyah Bidvaro, or said Barich Rachmana Malka Marei Dehai Pita ("Blessed is the Merciful One, King, Master of this bread") — he has fulfilled his obligation.

If people were riding and they decided to eat they constitute a single group even though each person eats from his own loaf as long as they are all standing in a single location. If they were eating as the animals were walking they do not constitute a single group. If they were eating spread out in a field they do not form a single group even if they are eat- ing at the same time and from a single loaf of bread since they did not set themselves in their place.

If they were riding and said, "Let us eat," then even if each one eats from his own loaf and they did not dismount from their animals, they are considered joined (for purposes such as zimun)—since they are standing in one place. But if they are eating while walking, they are not considered joined. And if they are eating scattered and separated in a field—even if they are all eating at the same time and from the same loaf—since they did not establish a place and are eating while dispersed, they are not considered joined....

In a case where they did not establish a fixed place—where we say that each one recites the blessing for himself—if the one reciting the blessing intended to fulfill the obligation on their behalf, and they intended to be fulfilled by his blessing, then they have fulfilled their obligation.

If there are many participants at the table, the greatest among them breaks the bread. Gloss Rema: If they are equal and one of them is a Kohen, it is a mitzvah to give him precedence. But if the Kohen is an ignoramus and the other is a Torah scholar, the scholar takes precedence. And if the Kohen is also a Torah scholar, but of a lesser level than the other, it is preferable to give him precedence, but it is not an obligation (see also Siman 281 and Mordechai, chapter "Bnei HaIr", and Beit Yosef in Siman 135 in the name of the Rashba). And if there is a host among them, he is the one who breaks the bread, even if the guest is greater. [And the one reciting the blessing should begin by saying, "With the permission of my teachers and masters."] (Or Zarua and Beit Yosef in the name of Shibbolei HaLeket).

The participants at the table are not allowed to taste until the one who breaks the bread tastes first. However, it is permitted to give each one their portion before he eats. (Tosafot and Mordechai, chapter 3 of "Sha'alu"). If each person is eating from their own loaf, and not all are dependent on the loaf of the one breaking the bread, they are allowed to taste before him. But if it is Shabbat, there must be two loaves of bread in front of the participants, aside from what is in front of the one breaking the bread. In that case, they may taste before the one breaking the bread.
The one breaking the bread is not permitted to break the bread until the "Amen" is completed by the majority of those answering.

The one breaking the bread should first extend his hand to the dish to eat. However, if he wishes to show respect to someone greater than him, he is permitted to give the portion to that person first.

The one breaking the bread gives a slice to each person, and each person takes the slice in their hand. The one breaking the bread does not give it directly into the hand of the eater, unless it is during a period of mourning. (Beit Yosef and Abudraham in the name of the Rambam, chapter 7 of Hilchot Berachot, and Responsa Rashba). (The reference to "and she shall stretch forth her hand" indicates a symbolic gesture during mourning, where the slice of bread is handed in a specific manner during times of grief.)

One who is not eating cannot recite the HaMotzi blessing to fulfill the obligation of those eating. However, he can recite it for children, even if he is not eating with them, in order to train them in the mitzvah.

Even on Shabbat, when one is obligated to eat bread, his friend cannot recite the HaMotzi blessing for him if he is not eating. It is not permitted for him to bless others, even if he is not tasting the bread himself, except for the HaMotzi blessing on matzah on the first night of Passover and the blessing over the wine for Kiddush, both at night and during the day. Gloss Rema: One should eat the piece of bread that was broken for the blessing before eating any other bread, and it should be eaten with appetite, as it enhances the mitzvah. (Agar and Nishmat Yisrael in the name of Shibbolei HaLeket).

**On which types of bread the blessing is said.** Pieces of bread and a whole bread were before him, all from one kind – he recites the blessing on the whole one, even if it is a coarse (meaning: bread that isn't pure) and small bread and the pieces are pure bread and large. But if the whole one is barley and the pieces are from wheat, even if it is small, he places the piece under the whole one and breaks from both of them together. Gloss: And all this is when he wants to eat from both of them. But if he only wants to eat from one, he should break on it and should not be concerned for the second one, even though it's valuable or liked by him (Terumat HaDeshen, No. 32).

If 2 whole ones, from one kind, one large and one small, he recites the blessing on the large one. If a person has two half-pieces of bread, and he doesn't have a whole bread, he should connect them together with wood or with anything so that it shouldn't be seen, and it has the law of a whole one. And even on Sabbath, he could connect them.

Two buns that are connected to each other which were baked, and a piece of the one was cut off, and the second one remained whole – it is better to separate the piece from the whole one, so that it should look whole, rather than to leave it connected to it, even though it looks larger. Gloss: And he should not break from it at the place where it was connected to its "friend", for there it looks like a broken piece. Rather, he should break from its "whole" place. [Rabbi Yaakov Levi].

Barley bread and spelt bread – he should recite the blessing on the one from barley since it is from the 7 species, even though the spelt is nicer. Pure bread and coarse bread – he should recite the blessing on the pure one. And if both are pure, and one is whiter than the other, he recites the blessing on the whiter one.

A pure loaf of heathen's bread and a coarse loaf of Jewish bread – if he is not careful not to eat heathen's bread, he recites the blessing on whichever one of them that he'll want. And if he is careful not to eat heathen's bread, he removes the pure heathen's bread from on the table until after the blessing of "...Who takes out...". And if the house-owner is not careful not to eat heathen's bread, and his intent is to only eat heathen's bread during the entire meal because it's pure, but his household members ate from the impure Jewish bread, and both types of bread are placed on the table, he needs to break on the pure heathen's bread since he's the one who breaks and his intent is to only eat from that bread. And if the house-owner is careful not to eat heathen's bread, and a Jew who isn't careful with this is reclining with him at the table, since the mitzvah is imposed on the house-owner, he should break from the nice heathen's one. And since he was permitted to break, he was permitted for the entire meal. Gloss: And this only provided that that bread is liked by him. But if it's not liked by him without the prohibition of heathen's bread he does not need to give it precedence. (Terumat HaDeshen, No. 32).

Bread offered as dessert – one recites on it the blessing "...Who creates kinds of sustenance". And after it – a blessing embodying three. And if he ate from it an amount that others are accustomed to fix a meal on it, even though he was not satiated from it, he recites on it "...Who takes out..." and grace after the meal. And if in the beginning, his intent was to from it a small amount, and he recited the blessing "...Who creates kinds of sustenance", and afterwards, he ate an amount that others fix a meal on it, he should recite on it the grace after the meal even though he didn't recite "...Who takes out..." in the beginning. And if he ate an amount that others do not fix a meal on it, even though he fixes a meal on it, he only recites on it "...Who creates kinds of sustenance" and one blessing embodying three, for his mind is cancelled by that of every person.

Bread offered as dessert – there are those who explain: Bread that is made in the form of pouches that they fill them with honey or sugar and walnuts and almonds and spices. And they are what are called rusklayis rialkhsu. And there are those who say that it's a dough that he mixed into it honey or oil or milk or types of spices and he baked it – and that is that the taste of the mixture of the juices or the spices is recognizable in the dough. [And there are those who say that this is called absolute bread – except if it contains a lot of spices or honey such as kinds of sweets that are called lekach, that the honey and the spices are almost the main part. And so is the custom.]. [Rashi and Arukh and so can be explained in the opinion of Maimonides]. And there are those who explain that it is bread – whether spiced or not spiced – that they make them dry cakes and they chew them. And they are what are called biskunis. And the halacha is like the words of all of them, that all of these things are given the laws which we said regarding bread offered as dessert.

Bread rolls – those that have a thick mixture, that are called ublias – is absolute bread and one recites on it the blessing "...Who takes out..." and grace after the meal. And those that have a loose mixture and are very thin – that are called niblas – he recites on them the blessing "...Who creates kinds of sustenance" and one blessing embodying three. And if he fixed his meal on them, he recites the blessing "...Who takes out..." and grace after the meal. And if he eats them within the meal, not due to the meal, they require a blessing before them and not after them. But those thin biscuits that they put concoction on them – they are subordinate with respect to the concoction and the blessing of the concoction exempts them.
Absolute bread – even less than like an olive – one recites on it the blessing "...Who takes out...". But after it he does not recite any blessing, as long as he didn't eat the amount of an olive.

Khabitsa, which is crumbs of bread that are stuck together with broth: If it was cooked – if they contain the amount of an olive, even though it doesn't have the look of bread, one recites on it the blessing "...Who takes out..." and grace after the meal. And if they do not contain the amount of an olive, even though it appears that it has the look of bread, he only recites the blessing "...Who creates kinds of sustenance" and one blessing embodying three. And if it is not cooked, just that it's connected with honey or broth – if the pieces contain the amount of an olive, he recites on it the blessing "...Who takes out...", even if it doesn't have the look of bread. And if they don't contain the amount of an olive – if they have the look of bread, meaning that it's recognizable and known that it's bread, he recites on it the blessing "...Who takes out..." and grace after the meal. And if they don't have the look of bread, he recites the blessing "...Who creates kinds of sustenance" and one blessing embodying three. And if it is not cooked and not connected, but thinly crumbled, even though it does not contain the amount of an olive, and not the look of bread, he recites on it the blessing "...Who takes out..." and grace after the meal. [And see below, Chapter 184, how much is the amount of eating to bless on it the grace after the meal].

There is an opinion that says that crumbs that are placed into water, and the water is whitened due to the crumbs, the torita [meaning: as if he said "to'arita"; that is to say: the look of the bread] of bread has gone away, and one only recites on it the blessing "...Who creates kinds of sustenance" and one blessing embodying three.

There is an opinion that says that bread that is soaked in [red] (Mordecai) wine – one only recites the blessing "...Who creates kinds of sustenance" and one blessing embodying three. And it appears that his words are only said regarding crumbs or regarding pieces that each one does not have the amount of an olive.

Even something thats mixture (meaning: the kneading of the flour with dough) is thick, if one cooked it or fried it, one does not recite on it the blessing "...Who takes out...", even if it has the look of bread, and even if it was obligated in challah, for the blessing "...Who takes out..." only goes after the time of baking. And there are those who disagree and say that anything that the beginning of the dough is thick, and even if he loosened it afterwards with water and made it spongy [meaning: a dough which he kneaded it and made it in the form of a sponge] and cooked it in water or fried it in oil, one recites on them the blessing "...Who takes out...". And the custom is to be lenient. And a Heaven-fearing one should fulfill both opinions and should only eat by reciting the blessing on a different bread first. Gloss: All of this only refers to a case where it has, after baking, the look of bread [language of Tur and the decisors]. But if it doesn't have the look of bread, such as noodles that are called in German wrimslich, according to all, the blessing "...Who takes out..." is not recited on them, and not 3 blessings, for it is not called bread. But pashtida and kreplech are called the look of bread (Mordecai, Chapter "Each Time") and one should only eat them if he recited the blessing on other bread first. And all of this only refers to a dough that does not contain oil and honey and the like, just that it's fried in them. But if it was kneaded with them, its law was already explained by bread offered as dessert.

That which was scalded [meaning: like a kind of bread – it is scalded with boiling water] that afterwards one baked it in an oven is absolute bread and one recites on it the blessing "...Who takes out...". Gloss: And likewise, something thats mixture is loose, that one baked it in an oven without liquid – its law is like bread and one recites on it the blessing "...Who takes out..." and three blessings. And likewise, if one baked it in a stewpot without liquid [Tosaphoth and Rabbi Asher and Rabbi Nissim, Chapter "The Entire Time"; and Maimonides, Chapter 6 of The Laws of Challah; and She'iltot; and Tur]. And the bit of liquid with which the stewpot is smeared so that it shouldn't burn the dough is not called liquid [Haggahot Maimuniyyot, Chapter 3 of Laws of Blessings]. But something thats mixture is loose, and one fried it in liquid – according to everyone it is not bread [Tosaphoth and Rabbi Asher and Rabbi Nissim and Rabbi Yonah, Chapter "How Does One Recite Blessings"].

Truknin – meaning that a hole is made in a stove in which flour is placed and water is mixed in it and it gets baked there – one recites on it the blessing "...Who creates kinds of sustenance" and one blessing embodying three. And if he fixed his meal on it, he recites on it the blessing "...Who takes out..." and grace after the meal. But "trita" – meaning that flour and water are taken and are mixed together and are poured onto the stove and it spreads and gets baked – does not have the law of bread at all and one only recites on it the blessing "...Who creates kinds of sustenance" and one blessing embodying three, and even if he fixed his meal on it.

1Indian bread, which is bread that is baked with a skewer and is smeared with oil or with egg-water, and likewise, bread that is made for kutakh, that is not baked in an oven, but in the sun, one recites on it the blessing "...Who creates kinds of sustenance".

17 A pie which is baked in an oven with meat or with fish or with cheese – one recites on it the blessing "...Who takes out..." and grace after the meal. Gloss: And only provided that one baked it in an oven without liquid. But if he baked it in a frying pan with liquid, he should not recite a blessing on it, and one should not eat it, except during the meal, as was explained [his own opinion, and likewise wrote Shibbolei Leket].

Anything that is brought before a person that has a fragrance and the person desires it, one must give from it to the meal attendant immediately. And it is a pious practice to give to him immediately from every type. And one should not give to him while the cup is in his hand or in the hand of the host. [And this is specifically regarding the attendant, but regarding another person at the meal, it is permitted to give in this manner.] R' Yonah, chapter "Elu Devarim." And it is forbidden to give him a piece of bread unless he knows that he has washed his hands.
He should not give [food] to eat except to one whom he knows will recite a blessing. And some are lenient if he gives to a poor person as charity [Rabbi Yonah, beginning of chapter 'Elu Devarim'].

The servant recites the blessing "who creates the fruit of the vine" over each and every cup that is given to him, because he is like a king. He recites the final blessing only at the end. He does not need to recite a blessing over each piece of bread if there is an important person at the meal, since he knows they will give him all the bread he needs. But if there is no important person at the meal, he must recite a blessing over each piece of bread, just as he does over the wine. Rema: When two people are eating together, the servant may eat with them without asking permission, so that they may join together for zimmun. [See below, section 170:21]

**Rules of proper conduct that a person should observe during a meal. Containing 22 paragraphs: ** One should not converse during a meal, lest the windpipe precede the esophagus (i.e., food goes down the wrong way). Even if someone sneezes during a meal, it is forbidden to say "health!" to him. If people were reclining at a meal and one of them went out to urinate, he washes one hand that he wiped with, and he only washes in front of everyone so they do not suspect him of not having washed. Rema: And if he did not wipe, he does not wash at all unless he touched a soiled place. But if he relieved himself, he certainly requires washing. This applies to drinking, but for eating he washes even outside [their view], for they know that his mind is troubled (meaning that he is anxious and confused) and he will not eat without washing. And if he spoke with his companion and became engrossed [in conversation], he washes both his hands since he became distracted. Rema: And this requirement of washing for drinking applies only in the middle of the meal, for we are concerned that perhaps he will eat. But otherwise, washing is not required for drinking.

Two [people dining together] wait for each other at the bowl — when one removes his hand from the bowl to drink, his companion stops eating until he finishes drinking. But if there are three, the [other] two do not stop for the one [who drinks].

Each of the diners leaves a corner [of food] in the bowl, which is food for the servant. But when the servant pours from the serving pot into the bowl, it is not the practice to leave anything in the pot for his needs.
One may not stare at the face of someone eating, nor at his portion, so as not to embarrass him.
One who enters a home should do whatever the host tells him.
A person should not be irritable [meaning: angry or short-tempered] at his meal.
A person should not eat a piece of bread the size of an egg, and if he ate [such a piece] he is a glutton.

One should not drink his cup in one gulp, and if he drank [this way] he is a glutton. Two [gulps] is proper conduct; three [gulps indicates] he is of a haughty spirit. Gloss: However, a very small cup may be drunk in one gulp (Beit Yosef), and likewise a very large one in three or four times (Darkhei Moshe).

One should not eat garlic or onion from its head, but rather from the top, and if he ate [from the head] he is a glutton. Gloss: And one should not eat in a gluttonous manner, and should not hold the food in one hand and tear from it with the other hand. [Tur]
One should not bite a piece of bread and place it on the table.
A person should not drink two cups at once during his meal and then recite Grace After Meals, because it appears gluttonous.
When two are sitting at the table, the greater one extends his hand first, and one who extends his hand before someone greater than him is a glutton.

One who enters a home should not say "Give me to eat" until they say so. Gloss: A person should not say to his friend "Come and eat with me what you fed me," for this is like repaying a debt and it appears as if he loaned to him, and there is concern that he will feed him more, and there is in this an aspect of interest. But it is permitted to say to him "Come and eat with me, and I will eat with you another time," and it is permitted to eat with him afterward, even a greater meal. [Darkhei Moshe according to the Tur]
A person should not break bread over the serving dish, but one may wipe the serving dish with bread.

One should not collect crumbs and place them on the table, as this disturbs one's companion. One should not bite from a piece of bread and then place it before one's companion or into the serving bowl, for not everyone's disposition is the same.
One should not drink from a cup and then give it to one's companion, because of mortal danger.
One should not drink from a cup and then place it on the table; rather, one should hold it in hand until the server comes and give it to him.
One who enters a meal should not take his portion and give it to the server, lest some mishap occur at the meal. Rather, he should take it, set it aside, and afterwards give it to him.
Guests who enter the home of a host may not take food from before themselves and give it to the host's son or servant, unless they have received permission from the host.

The discerning people of Jerusalem would not recline at a meal unless they knew who was reclining with them, because it is disgraceful for a Torah scholar to sit beside an am ha'aretz (unlearned person) at a meal.
A server who was serving two people may eat with them even if they did not give him permission; if he was serving three, he may not eat with them unless they gave him permission.

After you have drunk and wine remains in the cup for your companion to drink, wipe the place where the mouth touched because of disgust, but do not pour it out because of bal tashchit (the prohibition against waste). After drinking water, pour some out as a gesture of respect. Rema: After all your eating, eat salt, and after all your drinking, drink water, as will be explained below in siman 179. It seems this applies specifically when there was no salt in the bread or in the foods eaten, and likewise when one did not drink a beverage containing water; but otherwise there is no concern. And thus is the custom: not to be careful about eating salt and drinking water after the meal, for the reason that has been clarified.

A person can use bread as they need to, as long as they do not ruin it, but they may not ruin it. Therefore, one may not leave raw meat on bread or pass a full cup over it, not lean a bowl on it… and do not use wine even for a mitzvah like hand-washing. And do not throw bread because it is disgrace to food. And just as one may not throw bread, so too it is prohibited to throw any food that will become distasteful as a result.
A person should not sit on a basket full of figs and dried figs, but he may sit on a round cake of pressed figs or on a basket full of legumes.

It is permitted to eat diysa (meaning: hulled wheat that is cooked) with bread in place of a spoon, provided that one eats the bread afterward. Those who are scrupulous eat a small amount of the bread each time they put it in their mouth together with the diysa. Rema: And the bread that remains afterward, one eats it.

Wine is drawn through pipes before the groom and bride, provided that he receives it at the mouth of the pipe. And they throw roasted grains and nuts before them in the summer months since they do not become repulsive, but not in the rainy season because they become repulsive. But confections—never.
Those who throw wheat before grooms must be careful to throw only in a clean place, and they should also sweep it up from there so that it will not be trampled upon.

**One who drinks or eats without a blessing. Containing 2 paragraphs** If one put a drink in their mouth without saying a blessing, they should swallow it and not say a first blessing (a before blessing). Rema: And there are those who say a blessing and so it seems is the core practice [Rashba, in the name of the Raavad, and the Rosh Chapter 3 and also Maimonides Chapter 8 laws of blessings]

If one put food in his mouth without reciting a beracha and it would not be repulsive to remove it he should spit it out and recite the beracha. If it would be repulsive he should move it to the side of his mouth and recite the beracha with the food in his mouth

**The Law of Intermediate Water-Washing. Containing 3 paragraphs: **Intermediate water-washing is optional, and this applies between one cooked dish and another, but between a cooked dish and cheese it is obligatory. (See Yoreh De'ah section 89) .
If one has only one cup [of wine], set it aside until following the meal, and bless upon it.

One need not bless following the meal's wine, since the Birkat HaMazon covers it. And it also covers the pre-meal wine consumed, even if one hadn't consumed it amidst the meal. And regarding the matter of pre-meal Havdallah wine, see section 299:8.

If one doesn't have wine, and drinks water or another beverage, one need not bless upon them, since they are considered as having come on account of the meal, since one doesn't eat without drinking. And even wine needs no blessing before it, except that it is significant enough that a blessing was established for it, but water or other beverages are not significant beverages and do not require a blessing. ....

Everyone blesses for oneself upon wine amidst a meal, even if they are dining together. gloss: since they are not able to answer amen. since they are concerned lest it were to enter the trachea before the esophagus. gloss: And there are those who say that if he said to them, "Pay attention, my masters" and they listen and pay attention to the blessing and don't eat, then they will answer amen, one blessing for all of them. And that's how we are accustomed.

**Laws of the blessing HaTov veHaMeitiv over wine. 6 sections:** If they brought them another wine, he does not recite borei pri hagafen but does recite HaTov veHaMeitiv over it. Rema: Even if he no longer has any of the first wine. (Beit Yosef) And it is not specifically when they brought a new wine — the same applies if they had two wines from the beginning, they recite HaTov veHaMeitiv over the second. Rema: This applies specifically when both wines were not before him together when he recited borei pri hagafen, but if they were both there together he need only recite borei pri hagafen, as will be explained in section 3. (D"E to reconcile the Tur with Mordechai, ch. HaRo'eh) (Beit Yosef)

One recites HaTov veHaMeitiv over any change of wine by default, even if he does not know that the second is superior to the first, as long as he does not know it is inferior. Rema: There is no distinction between both being new, or one new and one old. (Beit Yosef in the name of Tosafot, ch. HaRo'eh, Tur, and Terumat HaDeshen §34) And this applies even if he drank from it within thirty days. Some say that if one first drank red wine and they brought him white wine — even if it is of lower quality — he recites HaTov veHaMeitiv, since white wine is healthier for the body than red. (Mordechai, ch. Arvei Pesachim)

If they brought him poor wine and good wine together, he should immediately recite borei pri hagafen over the good wine and thereby exempt the poor wine — he should not first recite borei pri hagafen over the poor wine in order to then recite HaTov veHaMeitiv over it, for one should always bless over the primary and the more beloved item first.

One should only recite HaTov veHaMeitiv if there is someone else with him, as the blessing implies — good for him and benefiting his fellow — and the same applies if his wife and children are with him; but if he is alone, he should not recite it.

If many people are reclining at a meal, each one recites HaTov veHaMeitiv for himself, and one person should not recite it on behalf of all, since we are concerned that they may have the windpipe precede the esophagus when they answer Amen. Rema: But if they were reclining to drink without eating, one recites it on behalf of all. (See above, end of §174)

Wine from two barrels, both of the same type — if within forty days of the harvest it was placed in two separate vessels, they are considered two different types and one recites HaTov veHaMeitiv over it. If they were divided after forty days, one does not recite it, since it is all of one type.

**That bread exempts the appetizer. 1 section:** If one blessed over bread, it exempts the appetizer, meaning very finely crumbled bread mixed with soup or honey. If one blessed over the appetizer, it does not exempt the bread. Rema: If one blessed over the appetizer it exempts cooked dishes such as porridge and the like, and similarly if one blessed over a cooked dish it exempts the appetizer. (Gemara, ch. Keitzad Mevarkhim, and Rambam in his commentary to the Mishnah)

**Things that come during the meal and after the meal — what is their law. Containing 5 sections:** Things that come during the meal — if they are things that come on account of the meal, meaning things that are typically eaten as part of a fixed meal to accompany the bread, such as meat, fish, eggs, vegetables, cheese, porridge, and various salted foods — even if one eats them without bread they do not require a blessing beforehand, as the HaMotzi exempts them, nor afterward, as Grace After Meals exempts them. If they are things that do not come on account of the meal, meaning things that are not typically eaten as part of a fixed meal to accompany the bread, such as figs, grapes, and all kinds of fruit (see above 168:8) — if one eats them without bread they require a blessing beforehand, as HaMotzi does not exempt them since they are not part of the main meal; but they do not require a blessing afterward, since having come during the meal, Grace After Meals exempts them. If at the beginning of his eating he ate the fruits with bread, and at the end he ate bread with them, then even if in the interim he ate some without bread, they do not require a blessing even beforehand.

Things that come after the meal but before Grace After Meals — it was the practice in the times of the Talmudic sages that at the end of the meal they would withdraw their hands from the bread, remove it, and settle in to eat fruits and drink whatever was brought before them — whether things that come on account of the meal or things that do not come on account of the meal, they require a blessing both beforehand and afterward, as HaMotzi and Grace After Meals only exempt what is eaten during the main meal. This last ruling is not common among us, since we are not accustomed to withdrawing our hands from the bread until Grace After Meals.

If one fixes his meal's accompaniment upon fruits, the fruits are treated like things that come on account of the meal, and even if he eats the fruits at the beginning of his meal without bread he recites no blessing either before or after them. Some disagree, and therefore it is best that he first eat some of the fruits with bread — for then even if he afterward eats them without bread they require no blessing at all. Rema: And this applies even if he does not return at the end to eat bread with them, since the main fixed eating was upon them. (Beit Yosef in the name of Ri)
Even if the fruits were not before him at the time he blessed over the bread — since they come to accompany the bread, they require no blessing at all.

If after he blessed over the bread someone from another household that he does not depend on sent him a gift, and he had not had that gift in mind — even things that are typically brought to accompany the bread require a blessing, as in the law of one who changes his mind. (And I have not seen people careful about this, and perhaps the reason is that a person's default intention covers everything that is brought to him during a meal and see above Siman 206.)

**Which things are considered an interruption during a meal. Containing 7 paragraphs:** If one was eating in one house and interrupted his meal and went to another house, or if he was eating and his friend called him to speak with him and he went out to the entrance of his house and returned — since he changed his location he must recite a blessing retroactively for what he already ate, and then recite HaMotzi again and complete his meal. But if his friend spoke with him inside the house, even if he changed his spot from corner to corner, he need not recite a blessing again. (See below §273 — if he had in mind to eat in another place it is not called a change of location, provided both places are in the same house; and see above §184.)

Friends who were sitting to eat and went out to greet a groom or bride — if some of them remained behind, they return to their places and complete their meal without needing to recite a second blessing. If no one remained when they left, they must recite a blessing retroactively, and when they return they must recite a blessing again. The same applies if they were reclining to drink or eat fruit, for whoever changes his location has interrupted his eating, and therefore he blesses retroactively for what he ate and blesses again for what he is about to eat. One who changes his spot from corner to corner within a single house need not recite a blessing again. If one ate on the east side of a fig tree and comes to eat on the west side, he must recite a blessing. Rema: Some disagree with everything written in this section and hold that a change of location is only equivalent to a lapse of attention — therefore if one changed his location he need only bless before what he wishes to eat next, but not retroactively for what he already ate. (Tosafot, Rashbam, Rosh, Mordechai, ch. Erev Pesach, and Tur) This applies specifically when he did not leave some companions at the meal and ate things that do not require a blessing in their place; but if he left some companions, or even if he did not but ate things that do require a blessing in their place, he need not bless even for what he wishes to eat afterward. (Semak and Or Zarua) Therefore, one who interrupted his meal and went to another house, or was eating and his friend called him — even to the entrance of his house or to another place — when he returns to the meal he need not bless at all, since bread requires a blessing in its place according to all opinions. However, if he had a lapse of attention, when he returns he certainly must bless for what he wishes to eat afterward. (Beit Yosef and Rashba) There is no distinction between returning to the place where he ate and finishing his meal in a different place. (Rambam ch. 4 and Ran) This is the custom in these lands. Nevertheless, one should not initially leave his place without a blessing, since we are concerned he may forget to return and eat. (R. Manoach and Ran) However, for the sake of a passing mitzvah, such as the time for prayer arriving, it is permitted. (Kol Bo, Laws of Pesach, and see §184)

Some say that if one was in a garden and wished to eat from the fruits of each tree — since he blessed over one tree he need not bless over the others, provided that when he blessed he had in mind to eat from those others as well. But from garden to garden one must bless again, even if they are adjacent and even if when he first blessed he had all of them in mind.

If one ate bread in one place and then ate again in another place, he recites Grace After Meals only in the second place, as is the custom of travelers who eat while walking and then sit and bless at the place where they finish eating.

Some say that the seven species require a blessing after them in their place; some say this applies specifically to the five grain species. Gloss (Rema): Some say it applies specifically to bread alone. (Beit Yosef §184 in the name of Rashba and Hagahot Maimoniyot ch. 4)

One who remembered during his meal that he had not prayed and stood up and prayed — even if there is not enough time to finish his meal and pray, and he is obligated to interrupt and cannot eat until he prays — this is nevertheless not considered an interruption.

One who fell into a light sleep during his meal — this is not considered an interruption. Rema: The same applies if he interrupted for other voluntary matters, such as needing to use the facilities and similar situations.

**Which things are considered a lapse of attention during a meal requiring a new blessing. 6 sections:** If one finished his meal and washed his hands with the final waters, he may not eat or drink until he recites Grace After Meals. If he said "let us say the blessing" this constitutes a lapse of attention and he may not drink unless he first recites a blessing over it. Eating has the same law as drinking according to the Rosh; but according to Rabbeinu Yonah and the Ran, eating is different — even though he withdrew from eating, and even if the table was removed, if he wishes to return to eating he need not recite a blessing again, since as long as he has not washed his final waters he has not fully withdrawn from eating.
One who depends on another's table — even if he said "let us say the blessing" it is not considered a lapse of attention until the host says so.
If he did not say "let us say the blessing" and also did not wash his final waters — once he has taken the cup to recite the blessing it is considered a lapse of attention.
When a person enters his friend's house and there are many groups eating, and each one offers him a cup — some say he recites borei pri hagafen over each one, since each time he is reconsidering.
Guests invited to a host's home to eat various fruits, and they are brought to them one after another — they need only recite a blessing over the first.

If one ate any food and did not eat salt, or drank any beverage and did not drink water — by day he should be concerned about bad breath, and by night he should be concerned about both bad breath and croup (a choking illness). One who eats salt after his meal should not eat it with his thumb — as it is harmful for burying children — nor with the little finger — as it is harmful for poverty — nor with the index finger — as it is harmful for bloodshed — but rather with the middle finger or the ring finger. (See above §170 for why we no longer practice eating salt and drinking water.)

(3) Before washing his hands (for mayim achronim) he should clean the house, so that no crumbs remain and become disgusting in the water used for washing. Although it is permissible to destroy crumbs that do not have a kezayis, perhaps the servant/butler will be an am ha’aretz (i.e., unlearned), (and will consider) that is permissible for him to use (the crumbs), and (he) will also place crumbs that have a kezayis that are forbidden to destroy by hand. Therefore, the host/ba’al habayis should clean first. *** And now we do not practice this because we do not remove the table and we wash our hands outside the table where there are no crumbs and there is nothing to worry about.
**Laws of Mayim Achronim. Contains 10 paragraphs:** 1. Mayim Achronim (washing after a meal) is mandatory

2. Mayim Acharonim should not be done over the ground, rather into a vessel since ruach ra’ah rests on the water; if one does not have a vessel he should wash over small pieces of wood or something similar.

3. One does not perform netilah (ritual washing) with water so hot that the hand is scalded by it, because it causes the hands to blister [the bracketed gloss explains: mefa'af'in means meva'be'in, from the language of shechin ava'bu'ot — boils and blisters] and does not remove the grime
4. One does not need to wash any further than the second knuckle
5. One needs to lower the tips of his fingers down so that the dirt comes off

6. If those reclining [at the meal] are many — up to five, they begin [the washing] with the one who recites the blessing [i.e., the one who will lead birkat hamazon]. And if they are more than five, they begin with the least distinguished [literally: 'the smallest'] and wash in the order of their seating, and they do not honor one another [by deferring the washing, saying 'you first'] until they reach the final five. And once only five remain who have not yet washed, they begin [again] with the one who recites the blessing
7. One doesn't make a blessing on Mayim Achronim.

8. There are those who say that mayim acharonim do not require drying [of the hands afterward], but according to the Rambam, one dries [the hands] and afterwards recites the blessing [birkat hamazon].
9. Mayim acharonim — one may wash with any kind of liquid.

10. There are those who are not accustomed to perform mayim acharonim. And even according to those who follow this practice [of not washing], a person who is fastidious [istenis] and is in the habit of washing his hands after a meal — for him, [his] hands are considered mezohamot [soiled], and he must wash his hands before birkat hamazon.

**Laws of the cup for Birkat Hamazon and that it should not be defective. It contains 7 paragraphs:** Some say that Birkat Hamazon requires a cup even when one is alone, and one must wait for it and not eat if he does not have a cup to bless over, if he anticipates and it is possible that he will have one—even if this means passing the time of one eating period. According to this, if two people eat together, each must take a cup for Birkat Hamazon. And some say it is only required when there are three, and some say it is not required at all, even with three: Rema: nevertheless, it is an optimal mitzvah to bless over a cup (Ran, chapter Arvei Pesaḥim).

The cup for Birkat Hamazon must be of wine and not of other beverages, even if he established his meal over them. And if wine is not available in that place, and beer or other drinks are considered ḥemar medina (important local beverage), one may bless over them, except for water: Rema: regarding the custom in these countries to bless over beer, one should not protest, since there are opinions that a cup is not required at all, and furthermore, the primary ḥemar medina is beer, and people establish their meals upon it. And even though wine is found in the city, it is still not considered readily available for this purpose, as it is expensive and not feasible to purchase wine for every meal to bless over. Nonetheless, it is an optimal mitzvah to bless over wine (Darkhei Moshe). Some are meticulous, when blessing alone over wine, not to hold the cup in their hand but to place it on the table before them, and this practice is proper according to the Kabbalah (Beit Yosef)

The cup must not be defective; if someone drank from it, it is defective. But if he poured from it into his hand or another vessel, it is not an issue. Even if he drank from the jug or a small barrel, it is considered defective. But if he drank from a large wooden barrel, one need not be particular. There is an opinion that even defective water is invalid to mix into the cup for a blessing.
If the cups of those who were lounging were unfit, it is necessary to put from the cup of blessing into them. And there is someone who says it is not necessary.

If wine from a defective cup was poured back into the wine jug, the wine in the jug remains valid, because each bit that was poured in becomes nullified as it mixes in (gradually and insignificantly).
People are able to fix an unfit cup by adding a little bit of wine; and even adding water to the cup can it be fixed.
In a pressing moment, we bless upon an unfit cup [of wine]

**One who blesses, how he should conduct himself with the cup of Birkat Hamazon. Containing 12 paragraphs.** 1. The cup of blessing for the Birkat HaMazon requires washing on the inside and rinsing on the outside. And if it was clean without residue on the cups, the rinsing and washing are not necessary.

2. The wine should be placed within the cup undiluted until reaching the Blessing of The Land, and then the wine should be mixed to acknowledge the praise of the land. Rem"a And there are some who say that if the wine is not strong, we need not dilute it with water [Tur]. And this how we are accustomed in these lands. And we take it out from the barrel for the purpose of a blessing [Tur in the name of Rashi]. And it seems for us that we only need to pour it from the jug that we guard of it wine for the purpose of a blessing; and it need not exactly be from a barrel. And this is how we are accustomed in these countries. And the cup for blessing should be filled up to the rim.
3. One needs to seek out a full cup [of wine] [for blessing over the Birkat HaMazon]

4. One receives the cup of blessing with two hands, and, when one begins blessing, one should lift it up with one's right hand without assisting it with one's left hand. Rema: And this [practice to not use one's left hand in elevating the cup of blessing] is specifically so that the left hand should not touch the cup; but, if one places the left hand beneath the right hand to help it, that is permissible. [Beis Yosef, in the name of the Shevulei HaLeket] And one should elevate it a fistbreadth from the ground if one was sitting on the ground. And if one was lounging at a table, one elevates it above the table a fistbreadth. And one sets one's eyes upon it, so as not to lose mindfulness about it. Rem"a: And, therefore [since one should place one's eyes upon the cup], one should not buy a cup - called a glueck - whose lip is thin, to bless upon it. And he sends it to one's wife so that she should drink from it.
5. There is one who says that if the blesser is lefthanded, the blesser should grab the cup in the blesser's right hand, which is everybody's left hand.

6. From when the cup is given to him to bless, the one blessing should not speak, and those reclining at the meal should not speak from the moment the one blessing begins. Not only while he is actually blessing — when they must listen and understand what the one blessing says — but even between one blessing and the next they should not speak. And if they transgressed and spoke between blessing and blessing, at a time when the one blessing was momentarily silent, they have fulfilled their obligation. (Rema): Even if the one blessing himself spoke. But if they spoke while he was actually blessing, they have not fulfilled their obligation.

7. It is proper that each of those reclining at the meal should recite quietly along with the one blessing every single blessing, and even the concluding formulas. (Rema): And he should finish slightly before the one blessing, so that he can answer Amen, as above in Siman 59. One does not give the cup of blessing except to one with a generous eye [Gemara, chapter Elu Ne'emarin].
8. Regarding interrupting Birkat Hamazon to inquire out of fear or out of honor, there is one who says that its law is like that of Tefillah.

9. One must sit at the time of blessing. Whether he was walking about his house when he ate, or standing, or reclining — when he reaches the point of blessing he must sit, so that he can concentrate better, and also so that he will not be reclining, which is a manner of haughtiness. Rather he should sit with awe. Rema: It appears to me that this is not specifically regarding the one blessing, but rather the same applies to all those reclining at the meal — they should not sit with levity but rather with awe. However, if they did not do so, even if he blessed while walking, after the fact he has fulfilled his obligation [Rambam, Chapter 4].
10. Some say that even al hamichya must be recited while sitting.
11. If one was walking and eating he does not need to sit to recite the beracha since his mind will not be settled.
12. It is forbidden to recite birkas hamazon while engaged in another activity.

Until when can one bless? Until the meal is digested in one's stomach. And how much is that measurement? The entirety of the time that one is not hungry on account of that eating. And from the time that one begins being hungry, even though the food hasn't been fully digested, we consider it to be as if it is fully digested. And, similarly, for the matter of eating fruits or drinking wine - if one is neither hungry nor thirsty, and they desire those fruits, they should bless [upon those fruits] if they do not know how much is left for their digesting.
Birkas Hamazon can be recited in any language
One needs to hear what he is reciting but if he does not hear he has fulfilled his obligation as long as he articulated the words
There is an opinion that that when a ba’al habayis is with his children and wife he must recite birkas hamazon out loud so they can discharge their obligation with his recitation
Even if one got significantly drunk to the point that the person is unable to properly speak, one is still able to bless the Birkat HaMazon.

If one blessed the Birkat HaMazon and [found] that there was feces near him or that he had been drunk, Tosafos and Rabbi Asher ben Yehiel were unsure if one needed to go back and re-bless the Birkat HaMazon, but not for urine; for that, one need not re-bless Birkat HaMazon.

**If Women and Children are obligated in Grace after Meals** Women are obligated to recite Grace after Meals. A doubt exists whether they are obligated from the Torah, and thus are able to fulfill the obligation of men (who listen to their recitation), or if their obligation is merely Rabbinical in origin, and thus can only fulfill the obligation for someone whose obligation is likewise merely Rabbinical. [See siman 199 concerning the laws of zimmun for women.]

Children are obligation by Rabbinical law (to recite Grace after Meals), in order to educate them. This teaching that a son may recite (the Grace) on behalf of his father only applies when the father ate an amount less that the point of satisfaction, thus making his obligation merely Rabbinical in origin.

**Details of the text of the blessing after meals. Containing 4 subsections.** Some say "Blessed is the one who satisfies the hungry". One should not say this, and the one who adds it detracts. If one said in place of the [first] blessing of nourishment, "Blessed is the Merciful One, Ruler of the World, Master of this bread", they have fulfilled their obligation. Some say that they must conclude "Blessed is the Merciful One, who Nourishes All."

In the [second] blessing of the land, according to the Ro"sh one should not say "Who has caused our ancestors to inherit a good and pleasant land...". Covenant and Torah - for behold, one says "For Your Covenant which is sealed in our flesh, and for Your Torah which you have taught us" - and it's enough [to have said it] just once. And the Rambam disagrees. [Rem"a: and the words of the Ro"sh are most important] .

If one did not mention covenant and Torah in the blessing of the land, or even missed only one of them, we return them. Rem"a: and women and slaves do not mention covenant and Torah, for women are not members of the covenant, and slaves are not members of the Torah. (Kol Bo)

If one did not mention the kingship of the house of David in the blessing of The One Who Rebuilds Jerusalem, we return them. Rema: And we say On the Miracles during Chanukah and Purim, before And On All..., and if one did not say these, we do not return them. (Tur). And in any case it is possible to say them in the rest of the May The Merciful One section, and say May The Merciful One Perform For Us Miracles Like They Did In Those Days... and so we are accustomed. (Kol Bo)

The text of the third blessing, laws of Grace After Meals on Shabbat, and one who errs in Grace After Meals. Containing 10 sections: After concluding with boneh Yerushalayim, one answers Amen after one's own blessing, because this is the conclusion of the Torah-level blessings, as HaTov veHaMeitiv is not Torah-level.

This Amen should be said quietly, so that people do not notice that HaTov veHaMeitiv is not Torah-level and come to treat it lightly. Rema: It seems this applies specifically when one is blessing alone and no one answers Amen after the other blessings; but when there is a zimun, others answer Amen just as they do for the earlier blessings, and even though the one blessing also answers, it is not so noticeable since others are answering along with him. This is the custom in these lands to say it aloud, even the one blessing himself when there is a zimun, and perhaps this is the reason.

One must mention the kingdom of the House of David in the third blessing, and one should not mention any other kingdom in it. One who says "and Your kingdom and the kingdom of David Your anointed" errs, for one may not equate an earthly kingdom with the heavenly kingdom. Similarly, one should not say Avinu Malkeinu in it. Rema: Some say that even when saying Ya'aleh veYavo one should not conclude with melech chanun verachum but should skip the word melech [Abudraham]. This is a sound reasoning, but I have not seen it practiced.

The text of this blessing opens with Rachem Hashem Elokeinu or Nachameinu Hashem Elokeinu and concludes with boneh Yerushalayim or menachem Tzion b'vinyan Yerushalayim. One should not change the text between Shabbat and weekdays, as the same text is recited both on Shabbat and on weekdays. Rema: Some say one recites boneh berachamav Yerushalayim, and this is the custom. (Mordechai, end of Berakhot)

On Shabbat one adds Retzei veHachalitzeinu, and on Rosh Chodesh, Yom Tov, and Chol HaMoed one says Ya'aleh veYavo. If one of these falls on Shabbat, one says Retzei veHachalitzeinu and then Ya'aleh veYavo, and one does not mention Shabbat within Ya'aleh veYavo, nor Yom Tov, Chol HaMoed, or Rosh Chodesh within Retzei veHachalitzeinu.

If one forgot to mention Shabbat, one says: Baruch Atah Hashem Elokeinu Melech HaOlam asher natan Shabbatot limnucha l'amo Yisrael b'ahavah l'ot ul'brit, Baruch Atah Hashem mekadesh HaShabbat. If one forgot to mention Yom Tov, one says: Baruch Atah Hashem Elokeinu Melech HaOlam asher natan yamim tovim l'Yisrael l'sason ul'simcha et yom chag ploni hazeh, Baruch Atah Hashem mekadesh Yisrael vehaZmanim. If Yom Tov falls on Shabbat, one says: asher natan Shabbatot limnucha l'amo Yisrael b'ahavah l'ot ul'brit, viyamim tovim l'sason ul'simcha et yom chag ploni hazeh, Baruch Atah Hashem mekadesh HaShabbat veYisrael vehaZmanim. All these blessings include God's name and kingship. This remedy of a supplementary blessing applies only if one remembered before beginning HaTov veHaMeitiv; but if one did not remember until after beginning HaTov veHaMeitiv, one must return to the beginning of Grace After Meals.

If one forgot to mention Rosh Chodesh — whether by day or by night — one says: Baruch shenatan Roshei Chodashim l'amo Yisrael l'zikaron, without a closing seal. This applies if one remembered before beginning HaTov veHaMeitiv. But if one did not remember until after beginning HaTov veHaMeitiv, one does not go back, because one is not obligated to eat bread in order to be required to recite Grace After Meals. Chol HaMoed has the same rule as Rosh Chodesh. Gloss (Rema): It is possible that nonetheless one should say it within the other HaRachaman passages, as was explained above at the end of §187 regarding Al HaNissim — though perhaps there is a distinction, since Ya'aleh veYavo contains mentions of God's name and one should not recite it in vain. So it seems to me, and this is the custom. If Rosh Chodesh falls on Shabbat and one mentioned Shabbat but not Rosh Chodesh, and did not remember until after beginning HaTov veHaMeitiv, one does not go back. If one also forgot Shabbat and remembered before beginning HaTov veHaMeitiv, one combines Rosh Chodesh with Shabbat and says: asher natan Shabbatot limnucha veRoshei Chodashim l'zikaron. If one already began HaTov veHaMeitiv, one returns to the beginning of Grace After Meals and mentions both Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh. Some say that if one forgot both Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh and remembered before beginning HaTov veHaMeitiv, one says asher natan Shabbatot limnucha veRoshei Chodashim l'zikaron and concludes with the Shabbat seal but not the Rosh Chodesh seal.
The third Shabbat meal has the same rule as Rosh Chodesh.

Three people who ate together on Shabbat or Yom Tov and forgot to mention the occasion, and must return to the beginning of Grace After Meals — each one blesses individually, since they have already fulfilled the obligation of zimun.
If one was eating and Shabbat ended, one still mentions Shabbat in Grace After Meals, as we follow the beginning of the meal. The same applies to Rosh Chodesh, Purim, and Chanukah.

Dans une maison de deuil, on dit : "Béni sois-Tu Hachem notre Dieu, Roi du monde, le Dieu, notre Père, notre Roi, notre Créateur, notre Libérateur, notre Sanctificateur, le Saint de Jacob, le Roi vivant, bon et bienfaisant, Dieu de vérité, Juge de vérité", etc. (voir Yoreh De'a, chapitre 379).

After concluding the Birkat HaMazon, one blesses "Creator of the Fruit of the Vine", then the blesser tastes [from the cup of wine]. After that tasting, others [at the meal] taste [from the cup of wine] if all of them are connected to one cup, and the blesser gives from their cup to empty cups in their hands. They should not taste from the cup of blessing until the blesser tastes. But, if they are not connected to that cup, they are able to taste prior to the blesser tasting. The blesser need not spill from their cup to the cups of their fellow diners, unless the cups of the fellow diners are unfit.
After one drinks the cup of Birkat HaMazon, one blesses the abbreviation of the three blessings.

There is a lack of agreement as to the amount of wine-drinking that obligates one in needing to say the concluding blessing, whether it’s sufficient with an olive's-volume or with a quarter-log. Therefore, one should be careful to drink either less than an olive’s-volume or a quarter-log in order to remove oneself from doubt. And, here, it's not possible to drink less than an olive’s-volume, since everything that requires a cup requires drinking from it like a cheeksful, which is a majority of a quarter-log. Therefore, one should drink an full quarter-log.

If the blesser does not want to taste, one of the fellow diners should taste [at least] the minimum amount [of wine], and two people's drinking does not combine to count for the minimum amount. And, nevertheless, it is a preferable performance that all of them should taste [from the cup of blessing].

When the diners are at a large meal, and they do not know whither the Birkat HaMazon cup reaches, each and every of those in doubt needs to bless Creator of the Fruit of the Vine if it arrives to them.

Laborers doing work for their employer should abbreviate the grace after meals so that they do not take themselves away from the work of their employer. How (do they abbreviate the grace after meals)? (They recite) the first blessing as established and the second they begin with "the blessing on the land" then include in it "He who builds Jerusalem" and conclude with "the blessing on the land". They do not recite the blessing of "The one who is Good and does good" at all. In what circumstances does this apply? When they are receiving payment for their work besides the meal (they are provided with). However, if they are not taking payment but rather are only provided with the meal they eat, they should recite all four blessings as established. This is also the case if the employer is eating with them, even if they are taking payment in addition to the meal, they should recite all four blessings.

When two people eat together, even though one may recite the beracha of hamotzi for the other, it is a mitzvah for each one to recite birkas hamazon for himself. This is true when both of them know how to recite birkas hamazon. If one knows and the other doesn’t the one who knows how should recite the beracha and the other will fulfill his obligation assuming he understands lashon kodesh but doesn’t know how to recite birkas hamazon. He must listen to each word that is recited....Rama: The one reciting the beracha must have in mind to discharge his friend’s obligation. Mechaber: If he does not understand he does not fulfill his obligation by listening. When three people eat together they may not separate and when two people eat together it is a mitzvah for them to search for a third to join their zimun. When four or five people eat together they may not separate since they are all obligated to make a zimuun. When the group is comprised of six they may separate since each group will make its own zimun and this is true until the group reaches ten. Once the group contains between ten and twenty people they may not separate until there are twenty since they will mention Hashem’s Name

Even if they were not initially established to eat together, but rather two people established a meal and afterward a third came and joined them, or one person established a meal at first and afterward the other two joined him — they are not permitted to separate, since they are considered fixed together at the end of the meal. However, in any case, if one eats with them without establishing (a meal) with them, they are permitted to separate — unless he is a servant. Rema : Nevertheless, even in any case where they are permitted to separate, it is preferable to make a zimun (invitation to bless) because “in a multitude of people is the King's glory” (Proverbs 14:28) (Beit Yosef).

If they were riding and said, “Let us eat,” even if each one eats from his own loaf and they did not dismount from their animals, they are joined (for zimun), since they stayed in one place. But if they were walking and eating — they are not joined. And if they were eating scattered and separated in a field, even if they are all eating at the same time and from the same loaf, since they did not designate a place to eat, they are not joined. Rema : The custom is not to perform a zimun in a non-Jew’s house, and the reason seems to be that they cannot establish themselves (for a meal) in a non-Jew’s house due to fear of the non-Jew, and it is as if they ate without establishing (a meal). Furthermore, there is concern for danger if they alter the wording of the blessing and do not say, “May the Merciful One bless this household.” Therefore, from the outset, they did not establish themselves, but rather each one intended to bless on his own. And thus the custom should not be changed, even if these reasons are not entirely sufficient — nevertheless, since the custom has already been established, it is as if they did not establish themselves together.
Three that sat down to eat and recited Hamotzi, even if they eat from their own loaf and they did not eat a kezayit, still they are forbidden to disband.

If three people come from three separate groups, each of which had three individuals, and these three (representatives) then joined together — if a zimun was already made in their original places (i.e., each group paused and two remained while the third led the zimun until saying “He Who provides…”), they can no longer perform a zimun together, even if they later eat together and finish their meal. But if no zimun was made in their original groups, they are obligated to make a zimun and are not permitted to separate — even if these three did not eat together after joining.

If there were three groups, each consisting of four people, and one person from each group left and joined together to form a new group, and the three who remained in each original group made a zimun — the zimun (obligation) is nullified for those who left, since their original groups already performed a zimun. The same applies if each original group had only three members, and one person from each group left before the zimun and the three who left joined together — and then someone joined each of the original two remaining in the groups to form three again and they made zimun — still, the zimun is nullified for the three who left, since their original groups already performed zimun, even though the zimun was made without them. Rema : If there were three groups, each with three people eating, it is forbidden for one person from each group to leave and join together for a zimun, since the two remaining in each group will no longer be able to make a zimun. But if each group had four people, then it is permitted for one person from each group to leave and join together for a zimun, and the remaining three in each group can make zimun in their original places (Beit Yosef in the name of the Rashba).

Three people that ate together, but forgot and benched by themselves, missed the mitzvah and they are not allowed to return and say the Zimun out of order. And also if two of them benched together but one forgot, the other two can have a Zimun with the third, even though he already benched, he is able to say "Baruch She'achalnu Mishelo," and they [the other two] fulfill their mitzvah of Zimun through this, but he [the third one] doesn't fulfill his Mitzvah, because he did it out of order. Rema: and if the third one did the Zimun with others, the first two cannot do the Zimun with him (Beit Yosef in the name of Rashba).

If three people ate together and one of them went out to the market [outside], they call out to him and inform him that they want to make the Zimun [the quorum for Grace After Meals], so that he will focus his intention, join them, and answer the Zimun blessing with them. They fulfill their obligation even though he does not come and sit with them. This applies specifically to three [people]. However, with ten, since they need to mention the Divine Name, they do not join together [to form the quorum] unless he comes and sits with them. [See later in Siman 200 regarding how far the blessing of the Zimun extends.]

If three people ate together as one, and not a single one of them knows the entirety of the Grace After Meals (Birkat HaMazon), but rather one knows the first blessing, one knows the second, and one knows the third—they are still obligated in the Zimun [the formal invitation]. Each one shall recite the blessing that he knows, and even if there is no one among them who knows the fourth blessing, it is of no consequence. However, they may not recite it by halves if one only knows half of a blessing, for a single blessing cannot be divided between two people.

1. Two groups that eat in one or two houses that can see one another join to form a zimun. If not [they do not see each other], they do not join. If there is one waiter [servicing] both groups, they join [to form a zimun]. This applies when they entered their meals to begin with with the intention of joining together [to form a zimun]. And there are those who say that if there is a public domain between the two houses, they do not combine in this matter.
2. When some of them ate in the house and some of them ate outside the house, if the one leading the blessing sits on the threshold of the house, he combines the two groups.

3. When the two groups combine, the one leading the blessing must be clearly heard by both groups. [Hagah] And each member of the groups says the after blessing himself. But, if they want to fulfill their obligation of the after blessing with the recital of the leader of the blessing, each one must listen to the entire after blessing [recited by the leader]. Without this, (according to all opinions) they have not fulfilled their obligation [to say the after blessing].
If one ate a forbidden item (even it is forbidden only by the sages), one cannot make a zimun on it or say a blessing on it, neither before or after it.
If one ate a forbidden item in a place of danger, he is allowed to bless on it.

Three ate together: one of them is careful not to eat gentile made bread and the other is not careful [ie he eats gentile made bread], or one of them is a Kohane and he eats challah. Even though the one who is careful [not to eat gentile made bread] can not eat [gentile made bread] with the one who is not careful, and [even though] a Yisrael cannot [eat challah] with the Kohane, since the one who is not careful [ie he eats gentile made bread] can eat [Jewish made bread] with the one who is careful, and [since] a Kohane is permitted to eat bread with a Yisrael, [when these eat together] they combine [to form a zimun]. But when there are Kohanim and a Non-Kohen eating together and the Kohanim are eating Challah and they are careful not to eat the gentile made bread, while the Yisrael [ie Non-Kohen] is eating gentile made bread, the Kohanim and Non-Kohen may not say zimun together. The same law applies when three take vows [not to benefit] from each other, i.e. they may not say zimun together.
A zimun cannot be made with a person that had less than a cazayit (olive's volume) of bread.

HAGAH: And there are some who say that one is not obligated to bless from a Torah level if one has not drunk [anything (at the meal)] and is thirsty. And it is good to be careful from the outset, if some of them have drank and some of them have not drank, that one who has drank blesses.
The waiter who ate an olive’s worth may be included in the zimun.
Nowadays, Cutheans are the same as idolaters and are not included in a zimun
Someone who is an absolute am ha’aretz is included in a zimun nowadays

4. A gentile is not included in a zimun. Even a convert who was circumcised but did not immerse may not be included in a zimun. Someone who is a full fledged convert is included in a zimun and he may recite birkas hamazon including the words Al Shehinchalta La'avoteinu
An onen (on a weekday), that is exempt from blessing, may not be included in a zimun.

We do not make a zimun with women, slaves or children but they may make a zimun by themselves. A zimun comprised of women, slaves and children should not be formed due to the promiscuity of the slaves, rather women should recite birkas hamazon by themselves and slaves by themselves but they may not use Hashem’s Name

Women have the option to form a zimun by themselves but when they eat with men they are obligated to answer and they fulfill their obligation by listening to the men Rem'a: even though they do not understand lashon kodesh
An androgynous makes a zimun with other androgynous, and he cannot be included in the zimun of men or women.
A tum tum never makes a zimun

A minor that has reached the age of understanding that he is praying to God can be included for the zimun for 3 and 10. Some say that a child cannot be included in a zimun until he reaches the age of thirteen and then he is assumed to be an adult who has produced two hairs. (Rosh and Mordechai Perek Shlosha Sheachlu and Tur) This is the custom and one should not deviate from it. Someone deaf or insane may be included in a zimun if he can concentrate and focus even though the deaf person cannot hear the beracha (Mahril)
One whom they excommunicated due to a sin is not included in a zimmun.

Laws of One Who Interrupts in Order to Bless — 2 paragraphs. Three people who ate together: one is obligated, even against his will, to interrupt for the two others and recite with them the zimun blessing. Even if he does not want to interrupt, they may perform zimun with him whether he responds or not, as long as he is still present. But two people are not obligated to interrupt for one, therefore the obligation of zimun does not take effect until they agree to interrupt for the one and to bless. If they do not wish to interrupt and he performs zimun with them, he accomplishes nothing. And if they do not wish to interrupt, he is also not permitted to bless and go out to the market until the two have finished and he performs zimun with them — for he has already become obligated in zimun, so how can he bless without zimun?

He only needs to interrupt until they say: "Blessed is He from Whose bounty we have eaten," (baroukh cheakhalnou mitouvo) etc. Rema: And some say that he must remain until they say: "Who nourishes all," (hazon et hakol) and this is the common custom (Rosh, Tosafot, R’ Yitzḥak in the name of the Baal HaHalakhot Gedolot, and the Tur). And if his intention was to return and eat bread, even if in the end he did not eat again — when he wishes to recite Birkat Hamazon, he begins from the blessing HaZan ("Who nourishes"), and all the more so if he actually did return and eat (R’ Yitzḥak, chapter "Three Who Ate") (Tur), and he may resume and finish his meal without repeating the opening blessing.
